# Focus

Click the Focus toolbar icon (the crosshair) to narrow the whole graph down to one note and its neighborhood - everything past a chosen number of hops away is hidden entirely, the same way Find path's result overrides the rest of the graph while it's showing.

## Using it

- Click the Focus icon to open the panel.
- Pick a note.
- Pick a hop depth - 1, 2, or 3.

The graph immediately shows just that note, its direct links (1 hop), their links in turn (2 hops), and so on out to the depth you picked - nothing else. Changing the hop depth while Focus is active updates the graph immediately, with no separate "Apply" step.

Focus is exclusive with Find path's result, an enabled filter's hiding, and a Diagnostics highlight - only one of these overrides the graph's normal contents at a time.

## Clearing it

Click "Clear" in the Focus panel, or close the panel with the "x" - both remove the restriction and show the whole graph again.

## When to use it

The Radial layout (see Layouts) answers a similar question - "how does the rest of my vault relate to this one note?" - by ringing every other note out by hop distance instead of hiding anything. Reach for Radial when you want the full picture with distance made visible, and for Focus when the vault is big enough that even that full picture is too much and you'd rather see only what's actually nearby.

# Fast 3D Graph

 **Explore your entire Obsidian vault as a fast, lightweight 3D force‑directed graph — smooth even with tens of thousands of notes.**
...
### What it is

Fast 3D Graph renders your whole vault as a 3D, real‑time, force‑directed graph. It is built around one goal: **show a huge number of notes beautifully in 3D, and keep it smooth.** Where the built‑in graph slows down on large vaults, this view stays fluid by splitting work across threads and leaning on the GPU.
...
* 🌐 **True 3D graph** of your vault, rendered with Three.js — nodes as GPU‑instanced spheres, links as a single line batch (2 draw calls total).
  * ⚡ **Built for scale** — **20,000 nodes render at ~75 FPS** , and it handles **50,000+**. The force simulation runs in a **Web Worker** powered by a **WebAssembly** physics core (AssemblyScript Barnes‑Hut, ~1.2× faster than the JS engine, with automatic JS fallback), so the camera and rendering stay smooth while the layout settles. Idle CPU drops to zero once it settles (alpha decay).
  * 🎨 **Cluster‑aware layout** — notes are grouped by folder or tag, with cohesion (pull same‑group together) and separation (push groups apart) forces, so communities are spatially distinct instead of one tangled ball.
  * ✨ **Flowing‑data hover effect** — hover or select a node and glowing particles stream along its links toward connected notes, with a gentle sequential color gradient.
  * 🖱️ **Interactive** — click a node to select it (its neighbors light up), click it again to open the note; hover for the title; drag to orbit; scroll to zoom.
  * 🔎 **Local‑graph mode** — focus on the active note and its neighbors up to N hops.
  * 🎞️ **Gentle auto‑rotation** for a presentable 3D feel (toggleable).
  * 🚫 **Respects Obsidian's _Excluded files_** setting (Settings → Files and links).
...
A real vault settling into its 3D layout:

_(If the player doesn't load inline,download/open sample.mp4.)_

20,000 nodes — still smooth:

_(Oropen 20k.mp4.)_

### Performance

Measured on a real machine (Apple Silicon). Render FPS is decoupled from the worker physics:

Nodes | Edges | Render | Physics tick (WASM) | Settle  
---|---|---|---|---  
~2,000 | ~5k | 60 FPS | ~5 ms | ~1 s  
~10,000 | ~25k | 60 FPS | ~38 ms | ~9 s  
20,000 | ~51k | **75 FPS** | ~81 ms | ~20 s  
50,000 | ~126k | fluid | ~268 ms | ~60 s  

Physics runs in a **WebAssembly** core (AssemblyScript), ~1.2× faster than the previous JS engine, with automatic fallback to JS if WASM is unavailable. Because the simulation lives in a Web Worker, a heavy tick never stalls the view — you can orbit, zoom, and click throughout while the graph organizes itself.

  * Run **"Open 3D local graph"** to focus on the active note's neighborhood.
  * **Drag** to orbit · **scroll** to zoom · **click** a node to open it · **hover** for the title.

results.summary:
# Reading the Obsidian graph view

The global graph is the screenshot everyone posts. It is the least useful view in the app.

At two hundred pages it is a hairball, and a hairball tells you nothing except that you have pages. What it is good for is spotting shape at a glance: isolated clumps, a single dominant hub, a scatter of unconnected dots around the edge.

## Local graph

This is the view that does work. Open a page, show the local graph, set depth to two.

You are looking for two things. What is one hop away should be obviously related; anything surprising there is either a decorative link to delete or a connection worth reading. What is missing at two hops tells you where the page is under-connected.

Reviewing the local graph of a page you just wrote is the fastest quality check there is, and it takes five seconds.

## Filters that make the global view usable

- Filter by type.-path:sources hides source pages and leaves the concept
graph, which is the part with meaning in it. Sources outnumber concepts
heavily and drown them visually.
- Groups by colour. Colour concepts, entities and synthesis differently. A cluster with no concept pages in it is a pile of sources nobody has processed.
- Orphan toggle. Turn orphans on deliberately, look at what appears, then fix or delete them.
- Depth and forces. Lower link force spreads clusters apart enough to see bridges.

## What to look for

Dots at the edge, connected to one thing. Failed ingests, usually. The source page was written and the concepts never linked back.

One giant node in the middle. A hub that has swallowed the graph. Split it.

Two clusters with a single connecting page. That page is doing real work. It is also fragile: if it is wrong, both clusters are wrong about each other.

A cluster you do not recognise. Usually the most interesting thing on screen. It means the vault has accumulated material on a topic you have not consciously been tracking.

## What the view cannot tell you

It shows that pages are connected, never why. Every edge looks the same whether it means "supports", "contradicts" or "mentioned once in passing".

That limitation is the entire argument for the next page.

# Graph View

Graph View is a [[Core plugins|core plugin]] that provides interactive network visualization of notes in your vault, representing notes as nodes and [[Internal links|internal links]] as edges between them. The graph allows you to explore the relationship structure of your knowledge base and navigate between connected notes visually.

For information about the internal linking system that powers the graph, see [[Internal links|4.2]].
...
## Architecture and Data Flow

Graph View operates as a visualization layer on top of the vault's link structure. It queries the metadata cache for link information and renders it using a force-directed graph layout algorithm.
...
## Graph Types

### Global Graph View

The global graph displays all notes in the vault that pass the current filter criteria. It is opened via the [[Ribbon]] icon or the Open graph view command en/Plugins/Graph view.md10
...
- Shows complete vault structure en/Plugins/Graph view.md88
- Circles represent notes (nodes), and lines represent [[Internal links]] en/Plugins/Graph view.md12-13
- Node size is proportional to the number of references to that node en/Plugins/Graph view.md15

### Local Graph View

The local graph displays notes connected to the currently active note up to a specified depth level. It is opened via the Open local graph command en/Plugins/Graph view.md88

Depth Control:

- Controlled via a slider at the top of the local Graph Filter Settings panel en/Plugins/Graph view.md90
- Each level of depth reveals notes connected to the notes from the previous depth en/Plugins/Graph view.md90

## Visualization Elements

### Nodes

Nodes represent individual files or tags in the vault.

Node Interaction:

- Hover: Highlights that note's connections en/Plugins/Graph view.md19
- Click: Opens the selected note en/Plugins/Graph view.md20
- Right-click: Opens a context menu with available actions en/Plugins/Graph view.md21

### Links (Edges)

Lines represent the connections between nodes.

- Arrows: Toggles whether to show the direction of each link en/Plugins/Graph view.md65
- Link thickness: Controls the line width for each link en/Plugins/Graph view.md68

## Filter System

The filter system determines which nodes and connections are rendered.

- Search files: Filters notes based on [[Search]] terms en/Plugins/Graph view.md40
- Tags: Toggles visibility of tags as nodes en/Plugins/Graph view.md41
- Attachments: Toggles visibility of non-markdown files en/Plugins/Graph view.md42
- Existing files only: Hides nodes that are linked but do not physically exist in the vault en/Plugins/Graph view.md43
- Orphans: Toggles visibility of notes without any links en/Plugins/Graph view.md44
- Excluded files: Files matching [[Settings#Excluded files]] patterns are hidden from the graph en/Plugins/Graph view.md47

## Groups and Color Coding

Groups allow you to distinguish notes using color based on search queries.

- New group: Create a new group definition en/Plugins/Graph view.md55
- Search box: Define the group using [[Search]] syntax en/Plugins/Graph view.md56
- Color circle: Assign a specific color to the group en/Plugins/Graph view.md57

## Display Settings

Controls the visual rendering of the graph:

- Text fade threshold: Manages label transparency based on zoom en/Plugins/Graph view.md66
- Node size: Global multiplier for node circle dimensions en/Plugins/Graph view.md67
- Animate: Initiates a time-lapse animation where nodes appear in chronological order based on creation time en/Plugins/Graph view.md69-82

## Physics Simulation (Forces)

Graph View uses a force-directed layout. The parameters can be tuned in the Forces section:

Force | Description 
---|---
Center force | Controls compactness; higher values create a more circular graph en/Plugins/Graph view.md75 
Repel force | Controls how much nodes push each other away en/Plugins/Graph view.md76 
Link force | Controls the tension of links (like a rubber band) en/Plugins/Graph view.md77 
Link distance | Controls the physical length of lines between notes en/Plugins/Graph view.md78 

## Navigation

Navigation within the graph is handled via mouse and keyboard:

- Zoom: Scroll wheel or+ and - keys en/Plugins/Graph view.md25...

results.summary:
September 21, 2020

## Shiny new things

- Graph view has been completely revamped.
- New options for filtering are now available. You can now:
- Filter files using same syntax as search. This can be especially useful to exclude certain folders like daily notes withpath:-"Daily notes".
- Choose to show#tags.
- Choose to show attachments such as images, audios, and PDFs.
- Choose to hide links to non-existent notes (only show existing files).
- Choose to hide orphan notes (files that do not have links, and is not linked to).
...
- New layout options are available to customize the graph to your vault.
...
- Choose to show arrows for links.
- Change the size of nodes and the thickness of links.
- Change the centering force, the repelling force, the link force, and the link distance.

- Local graph also has a few new option available.
...
- Choose to hide incoming or outgoing links.
- Choose to showing neighbor links. Disabling this option hides links between neighbor notes.

- You can now navigate the graph using the keyboard. Arrow keys to pan,+ and - to zoom, Shift to speed up movement.
- All graph options, including local graph depth and zoom level, are now persisted through restarts.
- Dragging to pan now has inertia. Zooming has been reworked to be much smoother.
- Graph colors now support custom CSScolor: rgba() values as well as opacity: 0.5.
- New graph CSS classes are.color-fill-tag, .color-fill-attachment, .color-fill-unresolved, and .color-arrow.
- Graph simulation is now done in a worker thread. This should make large graphs much more manageable.
- Several optimizations have been implemented to make the graph blazingly fast on vaults of all sizes. Many tricks are commonly used in modern day video games!
...
- Obsidian now supportsobsidian:// URIs. For the user manual, check out the help doc Advanced use > Using obsidian URI.

- Remember to use%20 to encode the space character, and %2F to encode the forward slash /.
- obsidian://open?vault=myvault will open the vault "myvault".
...
vault=myvault&file=mynote will open the file "mynote" inside the vault "myvault"/
...
path=%2Fabsolute%2Fpath%2Fto%2Fmynote will open the file at the absolute path "/absolute/path/to/mynote" assuming a vault exists for the one of the parent folders.
...
- The two shorthand from v0.8.15 are still available:
- The vault format:obsidian://vault/myvault.
- The vault + file format:obsidian://vault/myvault/mynote.
- The triple slash format for absolute paths:obsidian:///absolute/path/to/mynote or on Windows obsidian:///C:\path\to\mynote (forward slash also works).

# GitHub - jrayas/speed-graph: Obsidian plugin: a graph view that stays smooth on very large vaults (Rust/WebAssembly layout, canvas and WebGL2 drawing, optional 3D, shape layouts) · GitHub

# Speed Graph

A graph view for Obsidian that stays smooth on very large vaults. It works out the layout in the background, so zooming, panning and dragging never freeze, even with tens of thousands of notes.

_The default look: a plain graph in your theme's colours (1,000 notes)._

_One of the optional shape layouts: Honeycomb._

## How fast is it, compared with Obsidian's built-in graph?

Much smoother on big vaults. Here are the numbers for **25,300 notes and 59,867 links** :

Built-in graph | Speed Graph, first open | Speed Graph, reopened
...
First picture on screen | 0.77 s | 0.35 s | 0.06 s  
App busy while opening | 14.4 s | 3.1 s | 0.06 s  
Freezes over 50 ms while opening | 556 | 2 | 0  
Time per frame while zooming and panning | 124 ms (about 8 per second) | 8.3 ms | 8.3 ms  
Memory added | +420 MB | +9 MB | about 0  

**In plain words:** about 4 to 5 times less busy on the first open, about 15 times smoother while you move around, more than 40 times less memory, and a reopen in under a tenth of a second because the layout is saved. On 10,000 notes the same test gave 42 ms against 8.3 ms per frame. (8.3 ms is simply your screen's refresh rate: no dropped frames.)

**How far to trust this:** one MacBook, Obsidian 1.14.4, made-up vaults with random links, one run each, and the two graphs started with different zoom levels. The time to a fully calm picture is only about 1.5 times shorter on first open (10 s against 14.6 s); the big wins are smoothness, memory and the saved layout. Real vaults will differ. Method and every caveat: docs/comparison.md.

## What you get

 **Always on**

  * A fast, force-directed graph with a layout that is saved and restored.
  * Filters (search, tags, orphans, attachments, **excluded folders** ), colour groups, hover cards, drag notes to move them.
  * A **local graph** : turn it on, then click a note to see it with its neighbours; click another to move on.
  * Pan by dragging, or with the right or middle mouse button. Settings are behind the gear in the pane header.

**Off until you switch them on** (Settings → Speed Graph)

  * **Shape layouts:** pull your notes into a heart, spiral galaxy, brain, trefoil knot, spider, spider web, **honeycomb** , an **arc reactor** , or a **solar system** (your most-connected notes become the sun and planets). Shapes bring their own colours; turn "Use the shape's own colours" off to keep your normal look.
  * A **3D view** , moving **electrons** along links, a gentle **drift** so the graph feels alive, whole-graph **motion effects** (heartbeat, breathing, shockwave and more), **skins** , and zoomed-out **bubbles**.

**Make your own shapes.** A shape pack is one small file (data only, no code). Import it in the settings, copy any built-in one as a starting point. See docs/pack-format.md.

## Install

  * **Community plugins:** Settings → Community plugins → Browse → search "Speed Graph" (available once accepted into the directory).
  * **By hand:** put `main.js`, `manifest.json` and `styles.css` from the latest release into `<your vault>/.obsidian/plugins/speed-graph/`, restart Obsidian, enable the plugin. Needs Obsidian 1.13.4 or newer.

Then open it from the ribbon icon, or run **Speed Graph: Open graph view**.

**Formerly called Fast Graph** (releases 0.1.0 and 0.2.0). The name changed because another plugin already used that ID. If you installed one of those...

results.title: Data Visualization Challenge: The Struggle to Visualize thousands of Zettelkasten Notes and How I Solved It
results.summary:
# Data Visualization Challenge: The Struggle to Visualize thousands of Zettelkasten Notes and How I Solved It
...
When I started taking Zettelkasten notes in Obsidian, I never thought about scale.
...
For example, It saves me hours of research when writing a new article, I simply find the clusters formed on the relevant topic of interest in the obisidan graph view and then draft an outline based on the notes and relevant reference links using notebooklm. Then, Outline to draft is mostly combining those permanent notes and filling the parts with additional information as needed.

I crossed thousands of notes quickly, most of them grew out of my daily life, work as a technical writer and senior software engineer. Alongside these, I also used the same system for taking notes for hobbies and study of religious islamic text books, learning Arabic language, etc. which added an entirely different layer of content. Each note was atomic, small on its own, but together they formed a living network of ideas that kept expanding every day.

## The obsidian Graphview experience

At that point, my primary zettelkasten vault had become more than a collection of text; it was a dense web of knowledge that I wanted to see as a whole. That’s when I ran into a problem.

It seemed to me that Obsidian’s graph view is built for exploration, not for heavy-duty visualization. At a small scale it shines. You can see connections between notes instantly, zoom into clusters, and follow links that you might have forgotten. It works well when you have a few hundred or even a thousand notes.

The problem starts when the network grows too large. Rendering thousands of nodes and edges at once pushes the limits of how Obsidian handles the graph. The layout becomes sluggish even in a Mac mini M4, every movement lags, and eventually the app freezes.

Even when it loads, the graph is often too dense to be meaningful. You get a glowing ball of connections rather than a readable structure.

The Obsidian’s graph view, which I had once admired for showing connections at a glance, could no longer keep up. Opening the graph felt like asking too much of the app. The layout lagged with every zoom or pan, and eventually the entire view became almost unusable.

Splitting the notes into separate vaults gave me temporary relief, but as the collection kept expanding the problem returned. For example, I had to create separate vaults for notes related to Islamic studies alone, the following image is for the “smallest vault” containing notes on a single book named “Al Quran”. The core religious text book of Islam. There are currently 6236 notes in this vault in total.

The graph view was important to me, it was a way to spot hidden clusters and relationships that text search alone couldn’t reveal. For example, these are the relevant notes for the keyword charity from this vault.

Zooming further to reveal the actual subtle clusters formed here freezes the vault.

So I started looking for tools that could handle the weight of thousands of interconnected notes without grinding my machine to a halt. I tried most of the tricks found on reddit threads but no luck. Seemed like Obsidian’s graph engine isn’t designed for tens of thousands of relationships. For serious large-scale visualization, it quickly hits a ceiling.

## Searching for alternatives

Gephi could technically handle big networks, but importing notes and keeping the connections updated became tedious. Neo4j Bloom looked promising, but it required setting up a database and learning a new workflow that felt overkill for my use case. I also tested web-based tools like GraphXR and Kumu, but they either struggled with my dataset size, limited interactivity, or required sign up.

If I turn off the Graph view, rest of the useful Obsidian feature works without the lag. So, I only needed to replace the GraphView feature of obsidian. I needed a simple tool that could handle the scaling issue without freezing. I also tried Cosmograph. It wasn’t perfect, but it handled the data without freezing, let me pan and zoom easily, and gave a clearer sense of the network structure than anything I had tried so far.

## Exporting my permanent notes in Markdown to CSVs for Cosmograph visualization

Cosmograph expects two CSV files:

- Source – This one is for edges. (i.e. rows containing source -> target links)
